sections.h2: What is a quitclaim deed in Texas, and where does it fit?
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed is one of several deed types the county clerk records in Texas, alongside general warranty, special warranty, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds. The county clerk manual published through Texas Courts names it among the instruments filed in the deed records, and the filing office is the clerk's office covering the land.

That list is about the extent of what the official pages say about the form itself. No state agency page in this research explains how much protection a quitclaim gives a buyer, so treat anyone's promise about that as a question for a title company or a Texas real estate attorney. What the official sources do cover is how any deed gets signed, recorded and followed by later steps such as probate, tax and sale.

What a seller should take from this is short. A buyer's title company reads every deed in the chain. A quitclaim anywhere in that chain can prompt extra questions, so the sooner you know what is in your own chain of title, the fewer surprises appear after you sign a sale contract.

sections.h2: What else does the county clerk's office handle besides deeds?
sections.html:
The clerk's office does several jobs that matter when a house changes hands. The manual describes the county clerk as the county recorder for deeds, deeds of trust, liens and notices of foreclosure sale, as clerk of the commissioners court, and as the office that takes probate filings such as applications and small estate affidavits.

That means one phone call to the clerk can tell you whether a deed, a lien or a probate filing is on record against your property. State tax liens are also filed there: the manual says the Comptroller files notice with the county clerk, who records it in the state tax lien book. Before you promise a buyer clear title, ask the clerk for copies of everything indexed under your name and the previous owner's name.

  • Deed records: general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds.
  • Other recorded items: releases of deeds of trust, leases, contracts of sale and powers of attorney.
  • Probate filings and small estate affidavits.

sections.h2: What does a Texas deed need before the county clerk will record it?
sections.html:
The deed must be signed by the grantor and either acknowledged before an officer who can take acknowledgments or sworn, or signed before two subscribing witnesses. The clerk manual cites Property Code 12.001(b) for this rule and names a notary, a county clerk, a district clerk or a county court judge as officers who can take an acknowledgment.

  • Signature by the person giving up the interest.
  • An acknowledgment or sworn statement, or two subscribing witnesses.
  • Filing in the clerk's office for the county that covers the land.
  • The recording fees the clerk charges, listed below.

Recording is how the public record shows who holds an interest. A deed that stays in a drawer does not appear in the clerk's records, and a later buyer or lender searching those records will not see it.

sections.h2: What will the clerk bill me to file a deed?
sections.html:
The 2023 manual lists a small base charge per page plus several smaller add-ons, itemized here. Your clerk's posted schedule controls, so phone the office before you file.

Recording fee items printed in the 2023 county clerk manual
ItemAmount printedAuthority cited
First pageFive dollarsLocal Government Code 118.012 and 118.013
Each added page or attachmentFour dollarsLocal Government Code 118.012 and 118.013
Each name over five to be indexed$0.25Local Government Code 118.012 and 118.013
Records management and preservation feeNot more than $10Local Government Code 118.011
Records archive feeNot more than $10Local Government Code 118.011
Records technology and infrastructure fee$2.00Local Government Code 118.011

A missing mailing address for the grantee can add $25, the manual says. A commissioners court may direct the clerk to waive real property recording fees for buyers using certain federal or state grant programs.

sections.h2: Can a quitclaim deed move a house out of an estate?
sections.html:
Usually the route out of an estate runs through the probate paperwork, and a quitclaim signed by one heir does not replace it. The Texas State Law Library's deed guide describes which papers go on record for inherited real estate, depending on how the owner left it.

  • A recorded affidavit of death and a death certificate go with a transfer on death deed.
  • An administered estate needs an executor's or administrator's deed.
  • A muniment of title needs the court order and the will.
  • Without any of those, an affidavit of heirship may be used.

The same guide says the county cannot add heirs to the old deed. Whoever inherits can ask the clerk what the records show; the library's probate guides cover court options. A sworn affidavit of heirship carries no court verification, and the library notes that no law forces third parties to accept it.

sections.h2: What about a transfer on death deed or a Lady Bird deed instead?
sections.html:
Owners ask about both as an alternative to handing a relative a quitclaim. Per the State Law Library, a transfer on death deed passes real property without probate, can name charities as beneficiaries, can be cancelled by the owner, and must be on record at the clerk's office before the owner dies.

The library also describes the Lady Bird deed, an enhanced life estate deed, as one that lets the owner sell or mortgage without the beneficiary's consent. It adds that no official form exists. Because these deeds shape what a buyer can purchase later, a title company usually wants to see them before closing.

sections.h2: How do taxes and liens travel with a deed you sign?
sections.html:
Each January 1 a lien attaches to secure that year's property taxes, and the Comptroller says it lets a court foreclose even after the title changes hands. Whoever held title on that date owes the year's bill and can be sued for it after selling.

Per the Comptroller, no buyer gets clear title while delinquent taxes remain. Giving the house away by quitclaim does not wipe out that lien, so ask the tax office in your county for the status of every year before you list or transfer.

sections.h2: What should I do before selling a house I hold by quitclaim?
sections.html:
Order a title search or call a title company early, and read each deed in your chain of title. Quitclaims, handwritten deeds, missing signatures and unrecorded transfers are the items that slow a closing.

  • Pull the recorded deeds from the county clerk and check each one for a signature and an acknowledgment.
  • Check whether every co-owner or heir signed.
  • Ask the county tax office for tax status for all years.
  • Ask the title company what it needs to insure a buyer.

If the chain has gaps that the title company cannot clear, a Texas real estate attorney can say whether a corrective instrument or a court action is the right fix. Cash buyers who purchase as-is will often still require a clean enough record for a title company to close, so the same review applies.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed recorded with the county clerk in Texas?
faqs.a: Yes. The county clerk manual lists quitclaim deeds among the instruments filed in the deed records, at the clerk covering the real property, after the deed is signed and acknowledged or witnessed.

faqs.q: What does recording a Texas deed cost?
faqs.a: The 2023 clerk manual itemizes a charge per page, two records fees capped at $10 each and a $2.00 technology fee. Your clerk can quote the current schedule.

faqs.q: Can a quitclaim deed stop probate?
faqs.a: No source reviewed says it can. The State Law Library lists transfer on death deeds, muniments of title, administered-estate deeds and affidavits of heirship as the routes for inherited real property, so ask the clerk or a probate attorney before relying on a quitclaim.

faqs.q: Will a quitclaim erase unpaid property taxes?
faqs.a: No. The Comptroller says the January 1 tax lien lets a court foreclose even after ownership changes, and a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid.

faqs.q: Who can answer whether my quitclaim will pass title insurance?
faqs.a: A title company or a Texas real estate attorney. The official pages do not state how title insurers treat quitclaims, so the underwriter's own requirements control.
